title: Building an Elastic Enterprise for Human-Agent Collaboration
body_paragraphs: By Carlo Giovine and Vasu Gupta

Over the past decade, we’ve seen big changes happening for enterprise artificial intelligence (AI). Organizations have invested in chatbots and copilots designed to help workers with productivity, but these ambitions have moved from assistance to autonomy. Leaders now want to deploy systems that can plan and launch complex workflows all on their own.

Today, organizations are moving toward an elastic enterprise model, designed to reshape tasks, systems, and teams in real time. In an elastic enterprise, business processes become fluid, bringing together services, data, and human expertise to resolve business outcomes.
Scaling Agentic Capacity with Extended Reasoning

One of the biggest drivers for this change is the evolution of frontier AI models. Early AI operated on a one-step, immediate-response model. But today’s models use extended reasoning, giving them the ability to plan, self-correct, and evaluate their work before final output.

Models allowed to think longer across multiple scenarios can simulate different paths and refine their strategies. This extended reasoning lets models automate processes without constant human intervention.
Establishing an AI Delegation Framework
As agents take on deep-reasoning tasks, the move from automation to delegation closely mirrors how we interact with teammates every day.
To scale this safely, leaders of elastic enterprises focus on key decisions and protocols:
Transfer of authority and boundaries: Define the authority, limits, and system permissions to identify when the agent needs to escalate decisions to a human.

Accountability and verifiability: Be deliberate about verifying data. Automate tasks like code generation but require reputation scores or human-in-the-loop reviews for sensitive tasks like client communications.
Dynamic cognitive friction: If instruction is ambiguous or risky, the agent must pause for human review.
Designing a Secure Agentic Architecture

Elastic enterprises use architectures that align throughout the organization. Before deploying workflows, companies establish capability models and maturity assessments across infrastructure, data, applications, security, and operations.
These support agentic work at scale by identifying core areas that may be in need of development, including:
Agent building: Design and architecture for individual AI agents and complex multi-agent systems.
AgentOps: Framework for deploying, monitoring, and optimizing agent performance.
Data readiness: Agents connect securely to enterprise data assets.
Security and governance: Guardrails that identify and control potential AI system risks before they escalate.
Clearing Up Disconnected Data

Organizations that adopt an elastic enterprise model often must reengineer their workflows and infrastructures. Data simplification becomes a top priority as well, providing resources for teams and clean data for large language models.
This groundwork helps teams drive transformation through three strategic pathways:
Low-code (and no-code) accessibility: Lets employees deploy agents that understand natural language.
Plug-and-play integration: Connects agents directly to high-quality data architecture.
Pro-code necessity: Uses specialized agents to act as the bridge for modern agentic workflows.
Practicing Token Economics

When introducing AI agents, enterprises must develop a new approach to cloud FinOps that focuses on cost tracking and value governance. Because agents use token-based billing, organizations need a way to track total cost of ownership and value generated.
Working toward minimizing token waste and overall costs, elastic enterprises use specific methods for streamlining and refinement:
Speculative routing: Directing tasks and reasoning to fast models like Gemini Flash to handle high-frequency work at minimal cost.
Batching: Separating time-sensitive tasks from latency-tolerant workloads to use asynchronous batch application programming interfaces.
Guardian validation: Deploying specialized, low-cost agents to monitor outputs that break if they detect background looping or agent sprawl.
Inference pruning: Using research on deep-thinking tokens to prevent inefficient reasoning paths early on, matching premium model accuracy at half the token cost.
Adapting Elastic Talent and Human-over-the-Loop Collaboration

Agentic AI introduces a new category of digital talent into the workforce that requires new human roles and organizational culture. The relationship between workers and AI agents is a collaborative, elastic spectrum that evolves based on task, risk, and agent reliability.

In an elastic enterprise, human workers act as managers of digital talent through governance and boundaries. When a new agent is deployed, teams maintain human-in-the-loop oversight. As the agent builds trust and reputation score over many successful tasks, managers may scale back to human-over-the-loop involvement, monitoring as needed but focusing on actionable value instead.

Moving beyond legacy architectures to address the opportunities of AI agents is what makes elastic enterprises unique. More than just a change in technology, this transition is a shift in mindset and culture, giving teams a way to build an organization that can learn and lead in real time. With the elastic enterprise model, leaders can now readily prioritize agentic AI for their organization, turning ambition into autonomy.
Carlo Giovine is the leader of Delta, Google Cloud Consulting’s Forward Deployment Engineers team.
Vasu Gupta is the leader of Google Cloud Consulting’s Architecture and Industries team.
